questiontext.text: For an input defined as an integer in the range 1..100, how many equivalence classes does standard equivalence-class partitioning define, and which?

answer.text: Three: one valid class [1,100], plus two invalid classes (<1 and >100)

feedback.text: Correct — one class for accepted values, two for input that's too small or too large.

answer.text: Two: one valid class and one invalid class covering everything outside it

feedback.text: Values below and above the range fail for different reasons and are typically kept as separate invalid classes.

answer.text: One hundred: one class per accepted integer value

feedback.text: Equivalence partitioning groups values with the same expected behavior into one class, not one class per value.

answer.text: Two valid classes split at the midpoint, and no invalid classes

feedback.text: A single contiguous valid range doesn't need splitting, and out-of-range input still needs invalid classes.

generalfeedback.text: Standard equivalence-class partitioning for a bounded range [1,100] yields three classes: the valid class [1,100], and two invalid classes for values below the minimum and above the maximum.

questiontext.text: What are the six boundary values just inside, on, and just outside each end of an input range of [1,100], as used in Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)?

feedback.text: Correct — min-1, min, min+1, max-1, max, max+1.
That covers only the two on-points, missing all four neighboring off/near-boundary points.
This omits the min+1 and max-1 near-boundary points (2 and 99).
50 is a midpoint value, not a boundary — BVA targets the edges of the domain, not its center.

generalfeedback.text: BVA takes the minimum and maximum plus their immediate neighbors just inside and just outside the domain: for [1,100] that's 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101.

questiontext.text: Why does equivalence-class testing consider it sufficient to test just one representative value from each class?

answer.text: The uniformity hypothesis — all values in a class are assumed to trigger the same program behavior

feedback.text: Correct — the whole technique rests on that assumption.

answer.text: The exhaustiveness hypothesis — one value is assumed to prove correctness for all values

feedback.text: No such formal hypothesis exists; equivalence testing isn't exhaustive.

answer.text: Test values are assumed to be selected at random, so any one will do

feedback.text: Representative values are deliberately chosen (e.g., boundaries), not random.

answer.text: The independence hypothesis — each class is assumed unrelated to the others

feedback.text: Relationships between classes/variables matter for strong vs. weak testing; that's not why one value suffices per class.

generalfeedback.text: Equivalence-class testing relies on the uniformity hypothesis: the assumption that the program treats every value within a given class identically, so exercising any single representative value is as informative as exercising all of them.

questiontext.text: What class of fault does Boundary Value Analysis specifically target? (English term)

answer.text: boundary*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: off-by-one*

feedback.text: Correct.

generalfeedback.text: BVA targets boundary faults — the off-by-one style errors (e.g., using < instead of <=) that occur precisely at the edges of an input domain, which is why it concentrates test values there.

questiontext.text: What is the core idea of equivalence partitioning as a test-design technique?

answer.text: Divide the input domain into classes whose members are expected to be processed the same way, then test one value per class

feedback.text: Correct — it reduces the near-infinite input space to a small set of representatives.

answer.text: Test every possible input value exhaustively

feedback.text: Exhaustive testing is what partitioning is designed to avoid.

answer.text: Randomly sample inputs until a defect is found

feedback.text: That is random testing; partitioning deliberately structures the domain into classes.

answer.text: Measure how many statements each input executes

feedback.text: That is structural (code) coverage, not input-domain partitioning.

generalfeedback.text: Equivalence partitioning is a black-box technique that splits the input domain into equivalence classes (valid and invalid) and picks one representative per class, cutting the number of tests while keeping behavioral coverage.

questiontext.text: Why does Boundary Value Analysis concentrate test cases at the edges of an input range rather than in its middle?

answer.text: Programmers make off-by-one errors (e.g. < vs <=) most often at boundaries, so defects cluster there

feedback.text: Correct — boundaries are where relational operators are easiest to get wrong.

answer.text: Boundary values are faster for the program to compute

feedback.text: Execution speed is unrelated to why boundaries are chosen.

answer.text: Values in the middle of a range are never processed by the program

feedback.text: Middle values are processed; they're just less error-prone, so a single representative suffices.

answer.text: Boundaries are the only values users ever enter

feedback.text: Users enter all kinds of values; BVA targets boundaries because that's where faults concentrate.

generalfeedback.text: Faults cluster at boundaries because relational and loop conditions (<, <=, off-by-one) are most error-prone there; middle values are covered by a single equivalence-class representative.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 20, which value is the on point (the boundary value that lies inside the domain and satisfies the predicate)?

feedback.text: Correct — 20 satisfies x <= 20 and sits exactly on the boundary.
21 fails x <= 20; it is the off point just outside the domain.
19 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point, not on the boundary.
22 is an exterior point that fails the predicate, not the boundary value.

generalfeedback.text: The on point is the value on the boundary that lies in the domain. For x <= 20 the boundary value 20 satisfies the predicate, so 20 is the on point; 21 is the off point just outside.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 10, which value is the off point (the nearest value just outside the domain, which fails the predicate)?

feedback.text: Correct — 11 is the nearest integer that fails x <= 10.
10 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point, not the off point.
9 satisfies the predicate and is an interior point.
12 fails the predicate but is one step too far to be the off point.

generalfeedback.text: The off point is the nearest value on the other side of the boundary — just outside the domain. For x <= 10 the on point is 10 and the off point is 11.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 46, which value is the on point?

feedback.text: Correct — 46 sits on the boundary and satisfies x <= 46.
47 fails the predicate; it is the off point just outside.
45 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point.
48 is an exterior point that fails the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: For x <= 46 the boundary value 46 lies in the domain, so it is the on point; 47 is the off point just outside.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 37, which value is the off point?

feedback.text: Correct — 38 is the nearest value that fails x <= 37.
37 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point.
36 satisfies the predicate and is an interior point.
39 fails the predicate but is one step too far to be the off point.

generalfeedback.text: For x <= 37 the on point is 37 and the off point is the adjacent failing value 38.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 14, which value is the on point?

feedback.text: Correct — 14 satisfies x <= 14 and lies on the boundary.
15 fails the predicate; it is the off point.
13 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point.
16 is an exterior point that fails the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: For x <= 14 the boundary value 14 is in the domain, so it is the on point; 15 is the off point just outside.

questiontext.text: For the predicate x <= 21, which value is the off point?

feedback.text: Correct — 22 is the nearest value that fails x <= 21.
21 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point.
20 satisfies the predicate and is an interior point.
23 fails the predicate but is one step too far to be the off point.

generalfeedback.text: For x <= 21 the on point is 21 and the off point is the adjacent failing value 22.

name.text: Which value is in an invalid class

questiontext.text: An input field accepts an integer in the valid range 1..100. Which of these values belongs to an invalid equivalence class?

feedback.text: Correct — 0 is below the minimum, so it falls in the "too small" invalid class.
1 is the minimum accepted value, so it is in the valid class.
50 is inside 1..100, so it is a valid-class value.
100 is the maximum accepted value, so it is in the valid class.

generalfeedback.text: The valid class is [1,100]; anything below 1 or above 100 is invalid. Only 0 lies outside the accepted range here.

questiontext.text: A site admits users whose age satisfies age >= 18. Which value is the on point of this boundary?

feedback.text: Correct — 18 satisfies age >= 18 and sits exactly on the boundary.
17 fails age >= 18; it is the off point just outside the accepted domain.
19 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point, not the boundary.
16 is an exterior point that fails the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: For age >= 18 the boundary value 18 lies in the accepted domain, so it is the on point; 17 is the off point just outside.

name.text: Largest integer satisfying a strict bound

questiontext.text: For the strict predicate x < 50 over the integers, which value is the largest one that satisfies it?

feedback.text: Correct — with a strict <, the largest satisfying integer is 49, not 50.
50 does not satisfy x < 50 because the bound is strict.
48 satisfies the predicate but is not the largest such value.
51 is greater than 50, so it clearly fails the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: A strict inequality excludes the bound itself: for x < 50 the value 50 fails, so the largest satisfying integer is 49. This min/max +/-1 reasoning is exactly what BVA exercises.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes weak from strong equivalence-class testing when a program has several input variables?

answer.text: Weak testing covers each class at least once; strong testing covers the full cross-product of classes across all variables

feedback.text: Correct — strong is the combinatorially exhaustive version of weak.

answer.text: Weak testing covers the full cross-product; strong testing covers each class only once

feedback.text: This reverses the definitions.

answer.text: Weak testing applies only to Boundary Value Analysis; strong testing applies only to equivalence classes

feedback.text: Weak/strong is a distinction within equivalence-class testing itself, not a BVA-vs-ECT split.

answer.text: Weak testing tests only invalid classes; strong testing tests only valid classes

feedback.text: Both weak and strong testing normally cover valid and invalid classes; the difference is combination coverage, not validity.

generalfeedback.text: Weak equivalence-class testing needs only enough tests so each individual class (per variable) is hit at least once. Strong equivalence-class testing requires the cross-product of all classes across all variables, giving combinatorially more test cases.

questiontext.text: For a closed boundary (the boundary value itself is included in the domain), the off point lies just outside the domain.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the on point (the included boundary value) is inside the domain, so its paired off point is the adjacent value just outside.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: For a closed boundary the on point is inside the domain, so its paired off point is the adjacent value just outside it.

generalfeedback.text: Using the convention where the on point is the boundary value that lies in the domain (satisfies the predicate) and the off point is the nearest value just outside it: a closed boundary such as x <= b puts the on point (b) inside the domain and the off point (b+1) just outside. For an open boundary such as a < x, the smallest value inside the domain is a+1 (the on point) and the off point is the excluded boundary value a, still just outside the domain.

questiontext.text: In standard (non-robust) Boundary Value Analysis, which five values are selected for a single variable with range [min, max]?

answer.text: min, min+1, a nominal value, max-1, max

feedback.text: Correct — the two boundaries, their inside neighbours, and one nominal value.

answer.text: min-1, min, nominal, max, max+1

feedback.text: min-1 and max+1 are the robustness extensions, not part of standard BVA.

answer.text: min, nominal, max

feedback.text: This drops the min+1 and max-1 inside-neighbour values that standard BVA includes.

answer.text: min-1, min, min+1, max-1, max, max+1

feedback.text: That is the six-value robust set, not the five-value standard set.

generalfeedback.text: Standard BVA selects min, min+1, a nominal (typical interior) value, max-1, and max. Robustness testing later adds min-1 and max+1.

questiontext.text: Using the standard 4n+1 formula, how many BVA test cases are needed for a function with 3 input variables?

feedback.text: Correct — 4×3 + 1 = 13.
That is 4n; it forgets the single all-nominal test (+1).
15 does not match 4n+1 for n=3.
19 is the robust count 6n+1 for n=3, not the standard count.

generalfeedback.text: Standard BVA varies one variable at a time through its 4 non-nominal boundary values while holding the others at nominal, plus one all-nominal test: 4n+1. For n=3 that is 13.

questiontext.text: Robustness testing extends standard BVA by adding which extra values for each variable?

answer.text: min-1 and max+1 (values just outside the valid range)

feedback.text: Correct — robustness testing probes just beyond both boundaries.

answer.text: min+1 and max-1 (values just inside the valid range)

feedback.text: Those inside-neighbour values are already part of standard BVA.

answer.text: Two additional nominal values

feedback.text: Robustness testing adds out-of-range values, not more nominal ones.

answer.text: The midpoint and the mean of the range

feedback.text: Robustness testing is about out-of-range inputs, not central statistics.

generalfeedback.text: Robustness testing adds min-1 and max+1 to see how the program handles inputs just outside the valid range, giving seven values per variable and the 6n+1 count.

questiontext.text: Using the robust 6n+1 formula, how many BVA test cases are needed for a function with 2 input variables?

feedback.text: Correct — 6×2 + 1 = 13.
That is 6n; it forgets the single all-nominal test (+1).
9 is the standard count 4n+1 for n=2, not the robust count.
14 does not match 6n+1 for n=2.

generalfeedback.text: Robust BVA uses 6 non-nominal values per variable (adding min-1 and max+1) varied one at a time, plus one all-nominal test: 6n+1. For n=2 that is 13.

name.text: On point of an open lower boundary

questiontext.text: For the predicate 19 < x <= 25, which value is the on point at the lower boundary (the smallest value that lies inside the domain)?

feedback.text: Correct — with a strict lower bound, 20 is the smallest value that satisfies 19 < x.
19 fails 19 < x; it is the off point just outside the lower boundary.
21 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point, not on the lower boundary.
26 fails the upper bound; it is an off point at the upper boundary.

generalfeedback.text: For an open (strict) lower boundary 19 < x, the value 19 is excluded, so the on point inside the domain is 20 and the off point just outside is 19.

name.text: Off point of an open lower boundary

questiontext.text: For the predicate 27 < x <= 30, which value is the off point at the lower boundary (the nearest value just outside the domain)?

feedback.text: Correct — 27 is excluded by the strict <, so it is the off point just outside the lower boundary.
28 satisfies 27 < x; it is the on point at the lower boundary.
30 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point at the upper boundary.
29 is an interior point that satisfies the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: For the open lower boundary 27 < x, the smallest value inside the domain is 28 (the on point) and the excluded boundary value 27 is the off point just outside.

name.text: On point of a closed interval

questiontext.text: For the predicate 24 <= x <= 41, which value is the on point at the lower boundary?

feedback.text: Correct — 24 satisfies 24 <= x and sits on the lower boundary.
23 fails the predicate; it is the off point just outside the lower boundary.
42 fails the upper bound; it is the off point at the upper boundary.
30 satisfies the predicate but is an interior point.

generalfeedback.text: For the closed interval [24,41] the lower boundary value 24 is included, so it is the on point; 23 is the off point just outside.

name.text: Off point of a closed interval

questiontext.text: For the predicate 11 <= x <= 29, which value is the off point at the lower boundary?

feedback.text: Correct — 10 is the nearest value below the included minimum 11, just outside the domain.
11 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point at the lower boundary.
29 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point at the upper boundary.
20 is an interior point that satisfies the predicate.

generalfeedback.text: For the closed interval [11,29] the on point at the lower boundary is 11 and the off point just outside is 10.

name.text: On/off points for an open interval

questiontext.text: For the strict predicate x > 5, which pair correctly gives the on point and off point at that boundary?

answer.text: On point 6, off point 5

feedback.text: Correct — 6 is the smallest value inside the domain; 5 is excluded and lies just outside.

answer.text: On point 5, off point 6

feedback.text: 5 fails x > 5, so it cannot be the on point (the value inside the domain).

answer.text: On point 5, off point 4

feedback.text: Both 5 and 4 fail the predicate; neither is inside the domain.

answer.text: On point 7, off point 6

feedback.text: 7 satisfies the predicate but is interior, and 6 also satisfies it, so neither is an off point.

generalfeedback.text: For an open boundary x > 5, the boundary value 5 is excluded, so the on point (nearest value inside the domain) is 6 and the off point (nearest value outside) is 5.

questiontext.text: Why does standard BVA vary only one variable at a time (holding the others at nominal), giving 4n+1 tests?

answer.text: It assumes the single-fault hypothesis — failures are usually caused by one variable at an extreme, not several simultaneously

feedback.text: Correct — that assumption is what keeps the count linear in n.

answer.text: It assumes variables are always independent and never interact at all

feedback.text: BVA does not claim variables never interact; it just bets that single-variable extremes catch most boundary faults.

answer.text: It assumes the program has exactly one input variable

feedback.text: The 4n+1 formula is explicitly for n variables, not one.

answer.text: It assumes all boundary values are equally likely to be entered

feedback.text: Likelihood of entry is not the basis; the single-fault hypothesis is.

generalfeedback.text: Standard BVA rests on the single-fault (critical-fault) assumption: most failures stem from one variable at a boundary while the rest sit at nominal. Worst-case testing drops this assumption and combines boundaries, which is far more expensive.

questiontext.text: Using the standard 4n+1 formula, how many BVA test cases are needed for a function with 2 input variables?

feedback.text: Correct — 4×2 + 1 = 9.
That is 4n; it forgets the single all-nominal test (+1).
13 is the robust count 6n+1 for n=2, not the standard count.
5 is the standard count for a single variable (n=1), not two.

generalfeedback.text: Standard BVA needs 4n+1 tests; for n=2 that is 4×2 + 1 = 9.

name.text: Off point at an upper boundary

questiontext.text: For the predicate 5 <= x <= 17, which value is the off point at the upper boundary?

feedback.text: Correct — 18 is the nearest value above the included maximum 17, just outside the domain.
17 satisfies the predicate; it is the on point at the upper boundary.
16 satisfies the predicate and is an interior point.
4 is the off point at the lower boundary, not the upper one.

generalfeedback.text: For the closed interval [5,17] the upper on point is 17 and the off point just outside the upper boundary is 18.

name.text: Values per variable in robustness testing

questiontext.text: How many distinct test values does robustness testing exercise for a single variable with range [min, max]?

feedback.text: Correct — min-1, min, min+1, nominal, max-1, max, max+1.
5 is the standard BVA count; robustness adds min-1 and max+1, giving 7.
6 forgets one value: the robust set has seven (two boundaries, two inside neighbours, two outside neighbours, and one nominal).
9 is the standard BVA test count for two variables (4n+1), not values for one variable.

generalfeedback.text: Robustness testing uses seven values per variable — the five standard BVA values plus min-1 and max+1 — which is why the robust test count is 6n+1.

questiontext.text: Worst-case boundary testing takes the Cartesian product of each variable's five boundary values. For a function with 2 input variables, how many test cases does it produce?

feedback.text: Correct — 5^2 = 25, the full product of the five values per variable.
10 is 5×n; worst-case testing multiplies the value sets (5^n), it does not add them.
9 is the standard single-fault count 4n+1 for n=2, not the worst-case count.
20 does not match 5^n for n=2.

generalfeedback.text: Worst-case boundary testing drops the single-fault assumption and combines every variable's boundary values: 5^n tests. For n=2 that is 5^2 = 25.

questiontext.text: Robust worst-case boundary testing uses each variable's seven values (adding min-1 and max+1) in full combination. For 2 variables, how many test cases result?

feedback.text: Correct — 7^2 = 49.
25 is 5^2, the non-robust worst-case count.
14 is 7×n; robust worst-case multiplies the value sets (7^n).
13 is the robust single-fault count 6n+1 for n=2, not the worst-case count.

generalfeedback.text: Robust worst-case testing combines all seven robust values per variable: 7^n. For n=2 that is 7^2 = 49.

questiontext.text: How does worst-case boundary testing differ fundamentally from standard (4n+1) BVA?

answer.text: It abandons the single-fault assumption and combines the boundary values of all variables, growing exponentially (5^n)

feedback.text: Correct — combinations replace one-at-a-time variation.

answer.text: It uses fewer values per variable but more variables

feedback.text: It uses the same values per variable; the difference is combining them across variables.

answer.text: It tests only nominal values, never boundaries

feedback.text: Worst-case testing is entirely about combining boundary values, not avoiding them.

answer.text: It is always cheaper than standard BVA

feedback.text: It is far more expensive: 5^n grows exponentially versus the linear 4n+1.

generalfeedback.text: Standard BVA varies one variable at a time (single-fault assumption), giving 4n+1 tests. Worst-case testing combines every variable's boundary values, giving 5^n tests — exhaustive over boundaries but exponentially costly.

questiontext.text: In Ammann & Offutt's Input Space Partitioning (ISP), what is a characteristic?

answer.text: A feature of the input domain that is used to partition the domain into blocks

feedback.text: Correct — each characteristic induces one partition of the input domain.

answer.text: A single concrete test input value

feedback.text: That is a test value; a characteristic is the dimension along which values are partitioned.

answer.text: The expected output of the program

feedback.text: That is an oracle, not an ISP characteristic.

answer.text: A line of source code under test

feedback.text: ISP is black-box; a characteristic describes the input domain, not code.

generalfeedback.text: In ISP each characteristic partitions the input domain into blocks (for example "sign of x: negative / zero / positive"). Choosing good characteristics is the key design step.

questiontext.text: The blocks a characteristic splits the input domain into must satisfy which property?

answer.text: They must be complete (cover the whole domain) and disjoint (no value in two blocks)

feedback.text: Correct — completeness plus disjointness is exactly what makes the blocks a partition.

answer.text: They must overlap so every value appears in at least two blocks

feedback.text: Overlap violates disjointness; blocks of a partition are mutually exclusive.

answer.text: They must all contain the same number of values

feedback.text: Blocks need not be equal in size; they need only be complete and disjoint.

answer.text: There must be exactly two blocks per characteristic

feedback.text: A characteristic may have any number of blocks, as long as they partition the domain.

generalfeedback.text: For each characteristic the blocks must form a partition of the domain: complete (their union is the whole domain) and disjoint (mutually exclusive). Otherwise a value could be unclassifiable or ambiguous.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 3, 2, and 2 blocks. How many tests does All Combinations Coverage (ACoC) require?

feedback.text: Correct — 3 × 2 × 2 = 12, the product of the block counts.
7 is the sum 3+2+2; ACoC multiplies the block counts.
4 does not match the product of the block counts.
6 ignores one characteristic; the product over all three is 12.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC requires every combination of blocks across all characteristics, so the count is the product of the block counts: 3 × 2 × 2 = 12.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 3, 2, and 4 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests needed for Each Choice Coverage (ECC)?

feedback.text: Correct — ECC needs at least as many tests as the largest number of blocks in any one characteristic (here 4).
9 is the sum of the block counts; ECC can reuse blocks across characteristics in the same test.
24 is the product (All Combinations), far more than ECC requires.
3 is not enough to cover the characteristic that has 4 blocks.

generalfeedback.text: ECC requires each block of each characteristic to appear in at least one test. Because a single test picks one block from every characteristic, the minimum number of tests equals the largest block count — here max(3,2,4) = 4.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 3, 3, and 2 blocks. How many tests does Base Choice Coverage (BCC) require?

feedback.text: 8 is the sum of the block counts; BCC counts one base test plus the non-base blocks.
18 is the product (All Combinations), not the Base Choice count.
5 forgets the +1 base test: the total is 1 + sum of (blocks-1).

generalfeedback.text: BCC picks one base choice per characteristic (the base test), then varies one characteristic at a time through its remaining blocks: 1 + Σ(B_i - 1) = 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 6.

questiontext.text: What does Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC) require?

answer.text: Every pair of blocks from each pair of characteristics must appear together in at least one test

feedback.text: Correct — PWC covers all two-way block interactions.

answer.text: Every combination of blocks across all characteristics must appear

feedback.text: That is All Combinations Coverage; PWC only requires pairs.

answer.text: Each block of each characteristic must appear once, with no interaction requirement

feedback.text: That is Each Choice Coverage, which is weaker than PWC.

answer.text: Exactly two tests per characteristic must be run

feedback.text: PWC constrains block pairings, not a fixed number of tests per characteristic.

generalfeedback.text: PWC (2-wise) requires that for every two characteristics, every pair of their blocks is covered together in some test. It catches two-way interaction faults without the full ACoC explosion.

questiontext.text: An ISP model has three characteristics with 3, 3, and 2 blocks. What is the minimum number of tests any Pair-Wise Coverage set must contain?

feedback.text: Correct — at least the product of the two largest block counts, 3 × 3 = 9.
18 is the full All Combinations product; PWC needs far fewer than that.
3 (the largest single block count) satisfies Each Choice, not Pair-Wise.
6 is below the pairwise lower bound of 3 × 3 = 9.

generalfeedback.text: To cover every pair from the two 3-block characteristics you already need all 3 × 3 = 9 of their combinations, so any PWC test set has at least 9 tests — the product of the two largest block counts.

questiontext.text: Among ACoC, ECC, PWC, and BCC, which criterion subsumes all of the others?

answer.text: All Combinations Coverage (ACoC)

feedback.text: Correct — covering every block combination covers every pair, every base variation, and every choice.

answer.text: Each Choice Coverage (ECC)

feedback.text: ECC is the weakest of the four; it is subsumed by the others.

answer.text: Pair-Wise Coverage (PWC)

feedback.text: PWC subsumes ECC but not ACoC or (in general) BCC.

answer.text: Base Choice Coverage (BCC)

feedback.text: BCC subsumes ECC but is itself subsumed by ACoC.

generalfeedback.text: ACoC requires every combination of blocks, so it necessarily satisfies pair coverage, base-choice variation, and each-choice — it sits at the top of the ISP subsumption hierarchy (and is usually the most expensive).

questiontext.text: Which subsumption chain among the ISP criteria is correct (each criterion subsumes the next)?

answer.text: MBCC → BCC → ECC

feedback.text: Correct — Multiple Base Choice subsumes Base Choice, which subsumes Each Choice.

answer.text: ECC → BCC → MBCC

feedback.text: This reverses the direction; ECC is the weakest, so it cannot subsume the others.

answer.text: BCC → MBCC → ECC

feedback.text: MBCC subsumes BCC, not the other way around.

answer.text: ECC → PWC → BCC

feedback.text: ECC does not subsume PWC, and PWC does not subsume BCC (they are incomparable).

generalfeedback.text: Multiple Base Choice Coverage subsumes Base Choice Coverage, which subsumes Each Choice Coverage. Note that BCC and PWC are incomparable — neither subsumes the other.

questiontext.text: In Base Choice Coverage, how is the test set constructed?

answer.text: Pick one base block per characteristic to form a base test, then vary one characteristic at a time through its other blocks

feedback.text: Correct — that yields 1 + Σ(blocks-1) tests.

answer.text: Combine every block of every characteristic with every other

feedback.text: That is All Combinations Coverage, not Base Choice.

answer.text: Randomly select one block per characteristic for each test

feedback.text: BCC is systematic: a fixed base test plus one-at-a-time variations, not random selection.

answer.text: Use only the base test and nothing else

feedback.text: The base test alone does not exercise the non-base blocks; each must be varied in.

generalfeedback.text: BCC designates a base choice (e.g. the most common or important block) per characteristic, runs that base test, then changes one characteristic at a time to each of its non-base blocks while the rest stay at their base values.

questiontext.text: How are equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis usually combined in practice?

answer.text: Partition the domain into equivalence classes, then add boundary values at the edges of each class

feedback.text: Correct — partitioning finds the classes; BVA hardens the tests at their edges.

answer.text: Replace equivalence classes entirely with random boundary values

feedback.text: The two are complementary; BVA supplements, not replaces, partitioning.

answer.text: Use boundary values only for the invalid classes and ignore valid ones

feedback.text: Boundaries of valid classes are tested too; that is where most off-by-one faults live.

answer.text: Test only the midpoint of each equivalence class

feedback.text: That is plain equivalence partitioning without BVA; it misses boundary faults.

generalfeedback.text: The standard practice is to derive equivalence classes first, take one nominal representative from each, then apply BVA at the boundaries between classes — combining broad coverage with edge sensitivity.

name.text: Off point of a compound predicate

questiontext.text: Consider the compound predicate (x >= 10) && (x <= 20). Which single value is an off point of this predicate?

feedback.text: Correct — 21 fails the upper clause and lies just outside the domain, so it is an off point.
10 satisfies both clauses; it is the on point at the lower boundary.
20 satisfies both clauses; it is the on point at the upper boundary.
15 satisfies the predicate and is an interior point.

generalfeedback.text: The conjunction is equivalent to the closed interval [10,20]. Its on points are 10 and 20; the off points just outside are 9 and 21. Of the choices, only 21 is an off point.
